title: Towards Stable, Globally Expressive Graph Representations with Laplacian Eigenvectors

problem.claim: Laplacian eigenvector-augmented GNNs require proper handling of orthogonal-group symmetry to achieve stability and generalizability.

gap.claim: Naive O(p)-group invariant encoders for individual eigenspaces can lose expressivity and suffer numerical instability.

contributions.claim: A method uses Laplacian eigenvectors to generate stable and globally expressive graph representations.
The method uses learnable O(p)-invariant representations for each p-dimensional Laplacian eigenspace, built from orthogonal-group equivariant neural network layers.
The method handles numerically close eigenvalues smoothly to improve robustness against perturbations.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on various graph learning benchmarks report competitive performance.
The authors report particular potential for learning global graph properties.

narrative_sequence.summary: Laplacian eigenvectors can augment GNN node features as structural identifiers and global coordinates.
Orthogonal-group symmetry must be handled properly for stability and generalizability.
Naive invariant encoders may reduce expressivity and create numerical instability.
The paper proposes a stable, globally expressive representation method and reports competitive benchmark performance with potential for learning global graph properties.

source_observation.claim: Handling symmetry in eigenvector-derived features is central to representation stability and expressivity.

interpretation.claim: Symmetry-aware representations may avoid instability and expressivity loss caused by naive invariant encoding.

application.claim: When using eigenspace features, design representations that respect orthogonal-group symmetry and smoothly handle close eigenvalues.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish which graph-learning settings or perturbation regimes benefit most.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the benchmark datasets, baselines, metrics, or numerical results.
The abstract does not describe the model architecture or training procedure in implementation detail.
The abstract does not establish independent verification of the reported performance.
